cues.zh: 每次给学生讲课，我一直有点担心、也觉得所有人都该担心的一件事是：学生如果走上长期的编程职业生涯，可能会编程大约40年。
cues.en: Any time I'm giving a lecture to students, one of the things that I'm always kind of afraid of, and I think everyone should be, is that students, if they go on to a long programming career, will be programming for like 40 years.

cues.zh: 我已经编程40年了，我知道人们说在40年前成立的任何建议、信息或说法，往往过几年就不再成立，更不用说贯穿你整个编程生涯了。
cues.en: And I've already been programming for 40 years, and I know that any kind of advice or information or things that people say are true 40 years ago often aren't true even a few years after, let alone for all your entire programming career.

cues.zh: 所以这次讲座，我想试着搞清楚：关于软件架构，我能不能说出点什么——这主要是我日常做的工作，也是我思考最多的事情。
cues.en: So for this lecture, I kind of wanted to try and figure out, is there anything that I could say about software architecture, which is primarily what I work on day-to-day and what I think most about.

cues.zh: 有没有什么我见过的、能接近真正定律的东西——那种我认为永远不会被打破的东西——这样如果你学会思考它，并在看待软件架构以及一般架构时每天应用它，你就永远不必真正更新它。
cues.en: Is there anything I could say that I've ever seen that approximates an actual like law, like something I don't think will ever break, so that if you learn to think about it and apply it every day in how you view software architecture and architecture in general, that you'll never really have to update it.

cues.zh: 也许你会改进它，但你其实永远不需要更新它。
cues.en: Maybe you'll refine it, but you'll never really have to update it.

cues.zh: 所以，首先我想试着告诉你什么是定律，也就是我到底认为什么才算定律？
cues.en: So, first I want to try and tell you what is a law, like what do I actually consider a law to be?

cues.zh: 我们可以看看其他领域，很快就能弄明白。我们都知道物理学里的定律是什么。比如这里就是牛顿的万有引力定律。
cues.en: And we can look to other domains and figure this out really quickly. We all know what a law is in physics. Here for example is Newton's law of gravitation.

cues.zh: 这条定律非常简单。它说的是，两个物体之间的作用力，正比于某个常数乘以它们的质量，再除以它们之间距离的平方。
cues.en: And this law is very simple. It just says that the force acting between two bodies, right, is going to be proportional to some constant times the masses divided by the radius squared between them, right, the distance squared between them.

cues.zh: 这在当时非常具有革命性，我相信在它被提出的时候是这样，但它延续了一百多年，直到今天，我们仍在使用它。
cues.en: And this was very revolutionary. I'm sure at the time it was presented, but it lasted for for a hundred years or some on till today, and we still use it.

cues.zh: 如果你今天想在程序里做重力模拟，比如地面物体力学那种，你仍然会用这个，直到你要处理整个太阳系之类的情况，对吧？
cues.en: If you wanted to do gravity simulation today, in a program, in like terrestrial body mechanics, you would still use this until you got to like entire solar systems or something like that, right?

cues.zh: 所以这条定律确实被取代了，最终被爱因斯坦的相对论取代；我从来没把相对论敲进过程序，我用的是旧的那个，嗯，牛顿的牛顿定律。
cues.en: So this law did get replaced, eventually got replaced by Einstein's theory of relativity, which I've never typed into a program, I have used the old one, um, Newton's Newton's law.

cues.zh: 我从没用过爱因斯坦那种更新后的定律。
cues.en: I've never used Einstein's sort of updated law.

cues.zh: 所以对我来说，这才是定律的定义。它是我们如此确信的东西，比如牛顿万有引力定律，我们把它验证得如此充分，以至于即使后来发现它错了，它也不是真的错，更像是还不够完整。
cues.en: And so to me, that is really what the definition of a law is. It's something that we're so sure about, like Newton's law of gravitation, that we've proven out so well that even when it turns out to be wrong, it's not really wrong, it's more like not quite complete.

cues.zh: 而我们其实是在构造一个更微妙、更精细的版本，让它能涵盖更多东西。
cues.en: And we're sort of making some more subtle, more nuanced version that lets us capture more things.

cues.zh: 我们甚至不必停用旧的那套，因为它在所有场景里确实仍然有效。对我们当初用它做的那些事来说，它并不是谎言。
cues.en: We don't even have to stop using the old one because it really does still work in all the places. It wasn't a lie for all the things we were using it for.

cues.zh: 它仍然有效，只是现在想更进一步，你知道，做些改进。
cues.en: It still works, it's just now we want to go beyond, we, you know, make a refinement.

cues.zh: 所以问题是，软件里有没有类似的东西，对吧？
cues.en: So the question is, does software have anything like this, right?

cues.zh: 软件还很新，呃，物理学已经存在久得多，所以你会希望它到现在该有定律了，但愿如此，对吧？
cues.en: Software is very new, uh, physics has been around for much longer, so you'd expect them to have laws by now, hopefully, right?

cues.zh: 但、但是软件呢？
cues.en: But but what about software?

cues.zh: 我会说，你知道，现在下结论还太早，但确实有些东西看起来可能会成为定律。
cues.en: I would say that, you know, it's too early for us to say, but there are things that do look like they might turn out to be laws.

cues.zh: 比如，这是 Amdal 定律。它确实被称为定律，Amdal 定律，但在软件界人们什么都叫定律，所以这其实说明不了什么。
cues.en: For example, this is Amdal's law. It's actually called a law, Amdal's law, but in software people call everything a law, so that's not really much of an indication.

cues.zh: 被称为定律并没有什么标准，但它恰好就是，这就是 Amdahl 定律。
cues.en: There's no criteria for being called a law, but it does happen to be, it's Amdal's law.

cues.zh: 这是关于并行化程序的一个非常有趣的观察。
cues.en: And this is a very interesting observation about paralyzing programs.

cues.zh: 它说的是时间，执行时间，也就是你预期某个东西运行多久。
cues.en: What it says is the time, execution time, like how long you expect something to run.

cues.zh: 某个任务使用 N 个并行工作单元（比如 N 个线程）时，耗时将等于、也必须等于运行无法并行化部分所需的时间。
cues.en: The time for something using N parallel workers, so like N threads, for example, is going to be equal to, has to be equal to, the amount of time it takes to run the part that cannot be paralyzed.

cues.zh: 也就是根本无法拆成多个可同时完成的工作块的部分，无法并行化的部分，加上剩下的部分。
cues.en: So the part that simply cannot be broken up into multiple work, uh, pieces that can be done simultaneously, the part that cannot be paralyzed, plus whatever's left over.

cues.zh: 所以，单线程完成这件事的时间，减去无法并行化的部分，再除以线程数。
cues.en: So the time it takes to do the thing single threaded, minus the part that cannot be paralyzed, divided by the number of threads.

cues.zh: 这堂课你不需要理解这个，所以我不会讲得太细。
cues.en: Now you don't have to understand this for the lecture so, you know, I'm not going to go into to too much detail.

cues.zh: 但这个公式挺简单的，也很直观。你去看上十分钟，肯定就能明白。
cues.en: But it's a fairly simple equation and it's fairly straightforward. If you went and looked at it for 10 minutes, you'd totally get it.

cues.zh: 如果把这个含义画成图，你在哪儿都能查到。这张图是我从维基百科上拿的，是个很著名的结果。
cues.en: And if you graph what this means, you can look this up anywhere. I grabbed this chart from Wikipedia, just a well-known result.

cues.zh: 当你开始增加线程数，也就是增加处理同一个任务的计算单元数量时。
cues.en: As you start to increase the number of threads, so as you increase the number of computing components working on a task.

cues.zh: Amdahl 定律告诉你，执行这个任务所需的时间会迅速逼近、并且永远无法超过……
cues.en: Amdal's law tells you that the amount of time it takes to execute that task rapidly approaches and then can never exceed.

cues.zh: 执行单线程那部分所需的时间。
cues.en: The amount of time it takes to execute the single threaded part.

cues.zh: 为什么？因为那部分不会因为增加更多线程而变快。
cues.en: Why? Because that part doesn't get faster by adding more threads.

cues.zh: 这里你能看到几条线。一条对应完全可并行的问题，基本上就是95%可并行的情况，另一条对应可并行比例小得多的情况。
cues.en: And here you can see a couple lines. One is for if it's a perfectly paralize parallelizable problem, basically, if 95% of it is parallelizable, versus if like very much smaller amounts are paralizable.

cues.zh: 你能看到加速比渐近上会停在哪儿，对吧？
cues.en: You can see where you end up asymptotically on your speed up, right?

cues.zh: 所以你能看出为什么会这样。很简单。当线程或并行 worker 的数量趋于无穷时，这一项就直接消失了。
cues.en: And so you can see why this happens. It's very simple. As the number of threads or parallel workers goes to infinity, this term just drops out.

cues.zh: 因为 N 变得极大，所以它就不存在了。
cues.en: Because the N becomes extremely large, so it just isn't there.

cues.zh: 所以实际上，真正主导运行时间的就是不可并行的部分；因此，当计算机里的核心越来越多，
cues.en: So really, it's just the non-parallelizable part that dominates the runtime, so as you get more and more and more and more cores in a computer.

cues.zh: 或者 GPU 之类设备里的核心越来越多时，你会预期单线程部分变得占主导，因为不管我们怎么做，它永远不会加速。
cues.en: Or more and more cores in a GPU or whatever it is, you expect the single threaded part to become dominant because it will never speed up, no matter what we do.

cues.zh: 当然，这其实并不是在讲软件架构。
cues.en: But of course, that's not really about software architecture.

cues.zh: 我是说，它确实能让你了解一些优化方面的事，也可能影响你对软件架构的选择。
cues.en: I mean, it does tell you something about optimization and it might inform your choices of software architecture.

cues.zh: 我觉得这算是人人都该知道的东西，也确实值得学。
cues.en: It is sort of something I think everyone should know and I do think it's good to learn.

cues.zh: 它能经得起时间考验吗？谁知道呢？我的意思是，我们大概会得到更精细的版本。
cues.en: Will it stand the test of time? Who knows? I mean, we'll probably get more subtle versions of it.

cues.zh: 人们已经在这类系统里更多地考虑通信了。
cues.en: People already are sort of thinking about communication in there more.

cues.zh: 你可能还会往里面加别的东西。
cues.en: There's other things you would probably add to it.

cues.zh: 但这是很值得了解的东西，而且它确实有点像一条定律，因为我们知道，无论怎么做，你都不可能超过那条渐近线。
cues.en: But it's a very good thing to know and it does seem kind of like a law because we know you'll never be able to exceed that asymptote no matter what you do.

cues.zh: 这就是数学。
cues.en: That's just math.

cues.zh: 但架构有类似的定律吗？
cues.en: But does architecture have any laws like that?

cues.zh: 对吧？除了告诉你把程序拆成这么多块后最终能跑到什么速度，它其实并没有说明程序结构。
cues.en: Right? That doesn't really tell us anything about the structure of the program beyond the fact that here's the speeds it will end up running at if you broke it into this many pieces.

cues.zh: 但它能告诉我们的，真的就只有这些。
cues.en: But that's really all it tells us.

cues.zh: 所以，有些东西到处冒充“定律”，但它们其实并不是定律。
cues.en: So, there are things going around masquerading as laws, but they're really not laws.

cues.zh: 其中有些被称为定律，有些则不是。
cues.en: Some of them are called laws, some of them aren't.

cues.zh: 比如，你知道，如果你谷歌“软件架构定律”——我就这么干了，只是想看看人们会把什么称为定律。
cues.en: There's things like the, you know, if you googled software architecture law, which I did, just to see what people might call a law.

cues.zh: 你会看到帕累托原则之类的东西，它也叫 80/20 法则。它嘛，你知道，有各种不同形式。
cues.en: You'll get things like the Pareto principle, which is also called the 80/20 rule. It's like, you know, comes in various forms.

cues.zh: 80% 的时间花在 20% 的程序上，或者类似的说法。
cues.en: 80% of the time is spent in 20% of the program, or other things like that.

cues.zh: 它有各种各样的版本。
cues.en: There's all kinds of versions of it.

cues.zh: 但它不是定律。它其实什么都没告诉我们。
cues.en: But it's not a law. It doesn't really tell us anything.

cues.zh: 而且它也有点不准确。我是说，有时候会发生，有时候不会。它更像是一种模糊的“这种情况往往会发生”的说法。
cues.en: It's also just kind of not true. I mean, sometimes it happens, sometimes it's not. It's more of a vague this tends to happen kind of a thing.

cues.zh: 呃，这个，你知道，它也许……呃，但你知道，它在很多方面其实都不太可操作，所以它并不是真正的定律。
cues.en: Um, that, you know, it like like maybe, uh, but, you know, not it's not even really actionable in all that many ways, so it's it's not really a law.

cues.zh: 呃，你会学到像 SOLID 这样的东西，它就像面向对象编程的一串经验法则之类的。
cues.en: Um, you have things like solid which you'll get taught which are like this list of rules of thumb for object oriented programming or something.

cues.zh: 但再说一次，它不是定律；除了某些人认为不错的主意之外，它对软件架构没有任何说明。
cues.en: But again, it's not a law, it doesn't tell you anything about software architecture other than some things someone thought was a good idea.

cues.zh: 其中大部分我甚至都不觉得是好主意。所以它绝对不是定律。
cues.en: Most of which I don't even think are good ideas. So it's definitely not a law.

cues.zh: 这里面没有任何东西会真正导致软件出现某种真实的涌现属性，对吧？
cues.en: It doesn't there's no there's nothing in here that like causes an actual, you know, real emergent property of software to be told, right?

cues.zh: 就像定律那样。
cues.en: Like a law would.

cues.zh: 有些东西像 Pastell 定律——现在被叫作定律——还有 Amdal 定律，但它并不是定律。
cues.en: There's things like Pastell's law, which is now something called a law, Amdal's law, but it's not a law.

cues.zh: 这同样只是一个经验法则。
cues.en: It's just a again a rule of thumb.

cues.zh: 它的意思大概是：接受时要宽容，输出时要严格；再说一遍，这不是定律。
cues.en: It says something like you should be lenient in what you accept and stringent in what you output, again not a law.

cues.zh: 然后是 Brooks 定律，它确实是软件领域的定律，但同样，它还算不上架构层面的定律。
cues.en: And then there's Brooks Law, which actually is a software law, but again, it's still not quite architecture.

cues.zh: 但我确实想提一下，因为它很像 Amdahl 定律，多少和我们这里讨论的东西有关，而且它似乎是确实成立的。
cues.en: But I do want to mention it because much like Amdal's law, it's sort of a little bit related to what we're talking about here and it is something that appears to actually be true.

cues.zh: 所以在我继续讲真正想谈的定律之前，先快速说一下这个。
cues.en: So I'm quickly going to say this before I go on to the actual law I want to talk about.

cues.zh: Brooks 定律是 Fred Brooks 的一个观察；嗯，他很久以前写了《人月神话》。
cues.en: Brooks Law is an observation by Fred Brooks, uh, wrote The Mythical Man month, a long time ago.

cues.zh: 它算是第一本指出这些管理实践都基于“人月”这个概念的书；这个概念想象的是，人就像一种你扔向问题、就能让问题变快的东西。
cues.en: It was sort of the first book that said all these management practices are based on this concept called the man month, which imagines that a human being is just something that you throw at a problem and it gets faster.

cues.zh: 所以，你知道，如果我们想做出某个东西，往里投入更多人，只会让它做得更快。
cues.en: So, you know, if we have something we're trying to make, throwing more people at making it just makes it faster.

cues.zh: Brooks 在这本书里试图论证的观点，基于大量管理经验，以及当时行业正在经历的情况。
cues.en: And what Brooks tried to argue in this book was based on a lot of management experience and what the industry had been going through at the time.

cues.zh: 他基本上是想论证：你看，当任务很复杂，而且需要相互沟通时，
cues.en: He basically tried to argue that, look, when tasks are complicated and they involve intercommunication.

cues.zh: 最终你就没法做到这一点。
cues.en: You end up not being able to do that.

cues.zh: 这些是我从原书里截下来的图。
cues.en: He these are graphs that I grabbed from the actual book.

cues.zh: 我正好有这本书，就把它扫描了。
cues.en: I happen to own this book and I scanned it.

cues.zh: 第一张图展示的是，当你给项目加人、而且不需要沟通时，情况会是什么样。
cues.en: The first graph is what it looks like when you add people to a project and there's no communication necessary.

cues.zh: 就像他们在流水线上做某件事，不需要互相交流，直接做就行。
cues.en: So it's like they're just doing something on an assembly line, they don't need to talk to each other, they just do it.

cues.zh: 这看起来很符合你的预期，对吧？随着人数增加，效果会越来越好，但要知道，每加一个人——比如你加的第一个人，如果原本只有一个人干活，那时间会翻倍。
cues.en: That looks a lot, uh, like what you expect, right? It just keeps getting better as you go, but, you know, each person you add, you know, the first person you add, if you only have one person working, it doubles the time.

cues.zh: 再加下一个就不会这样了，对吧？所以这里有个自然的效率衰减。
cues.en: The next one won't, right? So you have a natural sort of power fall off there.

cues.zh: 下一张图展示的是，如果没法并行处理，会发生什么。
cues.en: Uh, the next graph is what happens if there's no ability to paralyze things.

cues.zh: 如果这些事只能串行完成，而且比如你只构建其中一个，那么给项目加人根本没用。
cues.en: If the things have to be done sequentially, and there you're only building one of them, for example, then adding people to a project doesn't do anything.

cues.zh: 他们只是干坐着，什么也做不了，对吧？
cues.en: They're just sitting around doing nothing, right?

cues.zh: 因为必须由一个人先把他手上的活全干完，交给下一个人，工作才能继续推进。
cues.en: Uh, because one person has to finish all the stuff they were doing and hand it to the next person before the work can proceed.

cues.zh: 所以在这种情况下，你别指望能有什么加速。
cues.en: So you don't expect any speed up in that kind of a case.

cues.zh: 嗯，渐近情况，也就是右边那个，说的是：增加人可以加快速度，但存在沟通障碍。
cues.en: Um, the asymptotic case, which is the one on the right, is the one where it says, look, you can make things faster by adding people, but there's a communication barrier.

cues.zh: 在复杂任务中，这些人必须相互交流。
cues.en: Those people have to talk to each other in these complex tasks.

cues.zh: 所以它不会一直趋近于零，而是会趋近于某个大于零的值，也就是协调这个任务所需的自然沟通成本。
cues.en: So rather than it continuing to go towards zero, it's going to go towards something higher than zero, that's whatever the natural communication cost is to coordinate this task.

cues.zh: 他们永远无法突破这一点。
cues.en: They're never going to get beyond that.

cues.zh: 除非我们有了蜂群思维技术，比如让埃隆·马斯克往我们脑子里植入芯片之类的，对吧？
cues.en: And not until we have hive mind technology from, you know, Elon Musk implants in our heads or something like this, right?

cues.zh: 最后，他展示了一张图，那是最坏情况。
cues.en: And then finally, he showed a graph that was like the worst case.

cues.zh: 就是沟通成本实际上可能一路增长，超过效率点。
cues.en: Is when the communication cost actually can just increase past the efficiency point.

cues.zh: 所以，如果我们给项目增加人手，而沟通效率不高，那么随着人员增加，成本实际上会比最初更高，对吧？
cues.en: So if we add people to a project and our communication isn't efficient, it will actually start costing more than it did originally as we add people, right?

cues.zh: 现在，如果你看看那条渐近曲线，它假设我们已经尽可能把沟通问题解决好，我们假定存在一个天然屏障：即使沟通已经尽可能做到最优。
cues.en: Now, if you take a look at the asymptotic one, where it's like assuming we got our communication worked out as well as we could, we assume there's a natural barrier where even if we're as optimal with communication as we can be.

cues.zh: 我们会碰到某个天然下限。如果你把它反过来想，并和 Amdahl 定律比较一下。
cues.en: We're going to hit some natural floor. If you just imagined like turning that around and comparing it to Amdal's law.

cues.zh: 你其实看到的是大致相同的表述。
cues.en: You're really kind of looking at roughly the same statement.

cues.zh: 这些表述讲的是：用并行工作者能把某件事做多快，并认识到存在一个根本性障碍。
cues.en: These are statements about how fast you can make something with parallel workers, and recognizing that there's a fundamental stumbling block.

cues.zh: 在 Amdahl 定律里，就是无法并行化的部分，也就是必须串行执行的部分；而在 Brooks 定律里，则是需要人员之间协调的部分，所以增加更多人手并不能带来预期那么多的收益。
cues.en: In Amdal's law's case, it's the part that cannot be paralyzed, the part that has to be sequential, and in Brooks law case, it is the part that it requires coordination between workers, which makes it so that adding more does not get you as much as you would have expected.

cues.zh: 对吧？
cues.en: Right?

cues.zh: 现在我们快接近了，因为这多少跟架构有关，但还不完全是架构。
cues.en: Now, we're getting close, because that sort of is about architecture, but it's not quite architecture yet.

cues.zh: 这就带到了我真正想谈的那篇论文——《How Do Committees Invent?》。
cues.en: So that brings us to the paper I actually wanted talked about, talk about, which is how do committees invent.

cues.zh: 这是一篇 1968 年的论文。
cues.en: This is a paper from 1968.

cues.zh: 发表在名为 Datamation 的杂志上，它就是发表在这本杂志上的；顺便说一句，这本杂志现在仍然存在。
cues.en: in a magazine called Datamation, it was published in this magazine, which by the way still exists.

cues.zh: 呃，也就是。
cues.en: Um, which is.

cues.zh: 这挺奇怪：它已经没有纸质版了，但在线上还存在。
cues.en: Which is odd, it doesn't exist in print anymore, but it exists online.

cues.zh: Datamation 是一本杂志，这篇文章就发表在那儿，因为《哈佛商业评论》之类的刊物不会登它。
cues.en: Datamation is a magazine where this was printed because the Harvard Business Review or something like this wouldn't print it.

cues.zh: 因为他们觉得它没能充分证明自己的结论。
cues.en: Cuz they didn't think it proved its conclusions.

cues.zh: 大概是论证不够有力之类的。
cues.en: strongly enough or something like that.

cues.zh: 这让我觉得有点好笑，因为这可能是我读过的最好的架构论文之一，绝对是。
cues.en: Which is kind of amusing to me because this is probably one of the best papers on architecture I've ever read, uh, bar none.

cues.zh: 所以在我看来，这倒也符合我对《哈佛商业评论》的看法——它没发表这篇文章。
cues.en: So it's, I guess fitting in my opinion of Harvard Business Review that it didn't publish it.

cues.zh: 这篇论文的作者叫 Melvin Conway，他来自 Caltech，当时在 Sperry Rand 工作，参与 Univac 项目，在 Rand 的 Univac 部门。
cues.en: So, it was published, uh, by a fellow named Melvin Conway, um, he was from Caltech and he was actually working at Sperry Rand, uh, on the Univac, uh, at the time, on Rand's Univac division.

cues.zh: 好的。
cues.en: Okay.

cues.zh: 让我先快速概述一下这篇论文讲了什么，然后我们再深入聊聊为什么我认为它很重要。
cues.en: So let me give you a quick overview of what this paper says and then we'll kind of go into why I think it's important.

cues.zh: 这篇论文非常好懂。听完讲座后如果有兴趣，我强烈建议去读一读。
cues.en: So this paper is very accessible. I highly recommend that anyone who's interested in this after hearing the lecture go read it.

cues.zh: 理解它并不需要很强的技术功底。
cues.en: It is not a paper that requires a lot of technical acumen to understand.

cues.zh: 它内容广泛、直观，而且写得非常好。
cues.en: It's it's broad, it's intuitive, and it's very well written.

cues.zh: 只不过它有点年代感，因为它是1968年的，所以你知道，它的文风比现在更讲究一些。
cues.en: So it's other than the fact that it's kind of a little old timey because it was 1968, so, you know, the the prose is a little more like sophisticated than it would be today, let's say.

cues.zh: 除此之外，它讲的内容非常容易理解。
cues.en: Um, other than that, it's very easy to understand what's being said.

cues.zh: 这篇论文说的是，过去有发明家，你知道，他们就是直接发明东西，对吧？
cues.en: What this paper says is there used to be, you know, inventors and they would just invent things, right?

cues.zh: 因为他们发明的东西相当简单，一两个人、五个人就能完成发明和设计。
cues.en: Because the things they were inventing were pretty simple, they could be invented and designed by one person or two people, five people.

cues.zh: 他们可以就待在一个房间里干活，最后另一端产出什么，能接受就行，对吧？
cues.en: They could just be in a room doing stuff, and then you got whatever came out the other end and it was fine, right?

cues.zh: 但当我们想做更复杂的事情时，比如——你知道的——阿波罗登月这种巨型项目，甚至是不那么了不起的东西，比如一台基础计算机。
cues.en: But as we want to do things that are more complicated, like the, you know, Apollo moon landing, these huge projects, or even things that are less impressive, like just a basic computer.

cues.zh: 呃，这些项目仍然需要大量的人参与，因为它们现在就是那么雄心勃勃，而且有些事根本不是一个人能指望独自完成的。
cues.en: Uh, still requires tons of people to work on these projects because they're that ambitious now, and there's things that no one person can really hope to accomplish by themselves.

cues.zh: 所以，要真正完成设计、发明这项任务，你在开始之前，真的必须先做一些事情。
cues.en: So in order to actually do the task of design, of invention, you must first do things before you start, really.

cues.zh: 而这篇论文指出，在你真正开始之前，必须有人先决定两件事。
cues.en: And what the paper points out is before you even really get going, somebody has to decide two things.

cues.zh: 第一，我们到底在造什么？
cues.en: One, what is it that we're actually making?

cues.zh: 这意味着它不能真的很开放。
cues.en: Meaning it can't really be very open-ended.

cues.zh: 我们必须先大致界定我们可能想造什么，并至少给它一个模糊的定义。
cues.en: We have to first kind of circumscribe what we might be trying to make, and give it some kind of at least vague definition.

cues.zh: 然后，我们必须决定推进这个设计的组织结构是什么。
cues.en: And then, we have to decide what the structure is of the organization that will pursue that design.

cues.zh: 对吧？
cues.en: Right?

cues.zh: 换句话说，我们需要某种方式——我们需要一家公司，对吧？我们需要身居其位的人，或者一批公司、一个联盟、委员会之类的。
cues.en: In other words, we're going to need some way of we need a company, right? We need we need people in positions or a collection of companies or a consortium or committees or something.

cues.zh: 如果我们想让20、30、40多人投入这项任务，就必须开始把他们分成小组。
cues.en: If we want to bring more than 20, 30, 40 people to bear on this task, we have to start breaking them into groups.

cues.zh: 而一开始，总得有人来决定这件事，或者一小群人来决定。
cues.en: And at the outset, someone's going to have to decide that or some small group of people have to decide that.

cues.zh: 论文接着又说，好吧，如果你要把事情拆分开，对吧？
cues.en: The paper then goes on to say, well, if you're going to break things up, right?

cues.zh: 当人数多到必须开始组建专注于特定主题的团队时，你就制造了一个协调问题，对吧？
cues.en: If you're going to have enough people that you have to start making teams that are going to focus on particular topics, you've created a coordination problem, right?

cues.zh: 现在你必须让这些团队彼此沟通。
cues.en: You now have to have those teams talk to each other.

cues.zh: 他们需要知道彼此在做什么，也需要能够相互协作。
cues.en: They need to know what each other are doing and they need to be able to work with each other.

cues.zh: 这本身就是一个实实在在的问题，独立于他们正在发明或设计的东西之外。
cues.en: And that's an actual problem in and of itself, separate from the act of inventing or designing whatever it is that they're making.

cues.zh: 而这篇论文中至关重要、我认为非常深刻的洞见，就从这里开始。
cues.en: And here begins the very crucial and what I think are profound insights from this paper.

cues.zh: Melvin Conway 告诉我们。
cues.en: Melvin Conway then tells us.

cues.zh: 一旦你选定了设计的某些方面，并决定把职责委派出去，对吧？
cues.en: Once you have chosen some aspects of the design, and you decide to delegate duties to it, right?

cues.zh: 比如你制定一份组织章程之类的，说这个团队要做某事，而那个团队可能实际上需要子团队来协调，对吧？
cues.en: Like you create an org charter or something, this team is going to do something and maybe that team actually needs sub teams to coordinate, right?

cues.zh: 一旦设计开始有了结构，真正由人组织起来的结构，每当你新增一个部分、对组织做一次新的划分，你其实都在预设某些设计是不必要的。
cues.en: Once you start having a structure, an actual human structure to the design, every time you make a new piece, a new breakdown of that organization, you are pre-supposing that certain designs are not necessary.

cues.zh: 你可能不是有意识这么做，但仅仅在两个团队之间划一条分界线，就意味着你在说：你在做的东西的设计，并不真的需要在这两个区域之间进行高带宽沟通，对吧？
cues.en: You may not be doing this knowingly, but just the act of drawing a dividing line between two teams means that you're saying that the design of the thing you're making doesn't really need to have a high bandwidth communication on between those two areas, right?

cues.zh: 就像汽车的轮胎和发动机要由不同团队来设计。
cues.en: Like the tires of the car and the engine of the car are going to be designed by different teams.

cues.zh: 所以我们是在预设发动机和轮胎不可能是一体的，对吧？
cues.en: So we're pre-supposing that the engine and the tire cannot be one piece, right?

cues.zh: 有时候这完全合理。
cues.en: And sometimes that's a perfectly reasonable thing.

cues.zh: 但另一些时候，这可能会砍掉设计空间中的一些部分，而最好的方案恰恰就在那里，对吧？
cues.en: But other times it may be lopping off parts of the design space that actually were where the best thing was, right?

cues.zh: 所以，这就引出了我认为非常精彩的一个结论。
cues.en: So, this leads to what I think is a really great conclusion.

cues.zh: 这大概是论文中最重要的部分，尽管它并不是这篇论文最广为人知的部分。
cues.en: Probably the most important part of the paper, although it's not the one it's remembered most for.

cues.zh: 也就是说，给定任意一种设计团队——这里指的是团队的组织方式——你其实已经可以断定，有些设计它是产不出来的，因为它无法以产出那种设计所需的频率，完成必要的沟通。
cues.en: And that is that given any design, team, like this is the organization of the team, you can already say that there are certain designs it cannot produce, because it is unable to do the communication that would be necessary at the frequency that it would need to do so, to produce that design.

cues.zh: 现在，呃，如果你再往前推一步——Conway 在论文里就是这么做的——他基本上是在说，这建立起了某种同态关系。
cues.en: Now, uh, if you take this a little bit further and Conway does in the paper, what he basically says is that sets up a sort of homomorphism.

cues.zh: 如果我们看一个组织的组织架构图，再看它产出的产品的结构，我们会预期它们基本上就是彼此的坍缩版本。
cues.en: If we look at the org chart for an organization and we look at the structure of the products that it produces, we would expect them to basically just be collapses of each other.

cues.zh: 意思是，如果我拿一个图和另一个图，我应该能对其中一个做小的节点合并或展开，然后得到同一个图。
cues.en: Meaning, if I took one graph and the other graph, I should be able to do some small node collapses or expansions on one or the other and get the same graph back.

cues.zh: 两者之间基本会有相同的结构，我们不会预期看到太大差异。
cues.en: There's going to be basically the same structure between the two of them and we're not going to expect to see much difference.

cues.zh: 好。
cues.en: Okay.

cues.zh: 所以这说明，我们会预期，对吧，组织只能成功设计出跟自身相像的东西。
cues.en: So what this tells us is that we would expect to see, right, organizations only able to succeed at designing things that look like themselves.

cues.zh: 而且，如果一个组织自身无法改变它的组织架构图，也就是说，组织内很难改变团队的组织方式，或者你很少这么做，或者有很多关于谁能跟谁沟通的规则，等等等等。
cues.en: And furthermore, that if an organization cannot itself change its org chart, meaning to the extent that it is difficult in an organization to change how teams are organized, or if you do so only very infrequently, or if there's a lot of rules about who can talk to who, etc, etc.

cues.zh: 你会把越来越多原本可能的设计方案排除掉。
cues.en: You will carve off more and more and more of the possible designs that you could have.

cues.zh: 以至于对于一个完全静态的组织架构图——比如无法改变、沟通线路非常固定、且不随时间变化的那种——他基本得出结论：它只会生产出自己的一个复制品。
cues.en: To the point where a completely static org chart, one that cannot change, one that has very defined lines of communication, for example, and that doesn't change over time, basically, he comes to the conclusion that it will just produce a copy of itself.

cues.zh: 这个组织产出的每个产品，都会长得像这个组织，对吧？
cues.en: Every product that comes out of that org will just look like the org, right?

cues.zh: 所以这就是康威定律。
cues.en: So that's Conway's law.

cues.zh: 康威定律简洁地表述就是：公司、组织、团队，无论细化到哪个层级，它们生产出来的东西都会具有和自身相同的结构，对吧？
cues.en: Conway's law as pithily stated is that companies, organizations, teams at any level of detail, they produce things that have the same structure as they do, right?

cues.zh: 与其说我们是在创造软件，不如说我们是在软件中创造自己的复制品，对吧？
cues.en: It's not so much that we're creating a piece of software as we are creating a copy of ourselves in software, right?

cues.zh: 用同样的图示结构。
cues.en: With the same kind of diagrammatical structure.

cues.zh: 为了让这个更直观一点，呃，对那些以前从未接触过康威定律的人——可能有很多人，因为它不常被讨论，所以不幸的是，真正认真想过它的人并不多。
cues.en: So to put this a little bit more visual, uh, for those of you who have never had any experience with Conway's law before, which is probably a lot of people because it doesn't get talked about that often, so not many people have really thought that much about it unfortunately.

cues.zh: 呃，希望这会改变，因为我觉得它非常重要。
cues.en: Uh, hopefully that will change because I think it's very important.

cues.zh: 但如果你想象我们坐下来，准备设计点东西。
cues.en: But if you imagine us sitting down, we're going to design something.

cues.zh: 首先我们得决定要设计什么。
cues.en: First we have to decide what we're going to design.

cues.zh: 对吧？
cues.en: All right?

cues.zh: 也许我们决定要设计一个操作系统。
cues.en: Maybe we decide we're going to design an operating system.

cues.zh: 然后我们开始想它需要哪些东西：哦，它得有互联网，还得有这个那个。
cues.en: And then we start to come up with the things that it needs. Oh, it's going to have to have like internet and it's going to have to have this and that.

cues.zh: 比如我们决定它需要的东西之一就是媒体。
cues.en: And like one of the things we decide it's going to need is media.

cues.zh: 它需要能播放媒体，得有视听功能，对吧？
cues.en: Like it needs to play back media. It has to have like audio visuals, right?

cues.zh: 于是我们决定，会从我们的主公司那边派一个代表团过来，里面会有一个团队，或者更可能是一个组织、一整个子组织，专门负责搞清楚这东西要怎么播放媒体，并编写这部分。
cues.en: So we decide there's going to be like a delegation from, you know, the the main, you know, our main company, there's going to be a team in there or or probably an org, a whole sub org, devoted to figuring out how this thing's going to play media and writing that.

cues.zh: 嗯，大概是因为我们在招人，会招音频的人做音频，视频的人做视频。
cues.en: Well, probably because we're hiring people, we're going to hire like audio people for audio and video people for video.

cues.zh: 我们最后很可能会把团队结构定成有一个音频团队和一个视频团队，对吧？
cues.en: We probably end up structuring the team as there's an audio team and a video team, right?

cues.zh: 而它们都归在媒体这个大类下面。
cues.en: And they're both underneath the media umbrella.

cues.zh: 音频团队可能又会分成播放音乐和播放音效，因为有时候这两者在某些方面不太一样，之类的。
cues.en: The audio team might be like split up into like playing music versus playing sound because sometimes those have different, uh, you know, aspects to them or whatever.

cues.zh: 呃，然后视频团队可能会比如分成 2D 和 3D。
cues.en: Uh, and then the video team might be like split into 2D and 3D, let's say.

cues.zh: 这只是给你一个非常基础的简单例子。
cues.en: That's this is just give you a very simple example of like very basic.

cues.zh: 今天任何组织架构图，比如公司里的，像 Google 之类的，都比这复杂得多。
cues.en: Any org chart today, like in a company, um, like Google or something is vastly more complicated than this.

cues.zh: 所以相比之下这非常简单，只是让你有个感觉，对吧？
cues.en: So this is like very simple by comparison, just to give you a flavor of it, right?

cues.zh: 如果我们坐下来做这件事。
cues.en: If we were to sit down and do this.

cues.zh: 我们最终期望看到的产品会是什么？
cues.en: What would we expect to see as a product at the end of the day?

cues.zh: 它不会是随便任意的东西。
cues.en: It would not be something that's just arbitrary.

cues.zh: 我们不会期望有，我不知道，会有某种用于播放媒体的 API。
cues.en: We wouldn't expect to have, I don't know, there'll be some API for playing media.

cues.zh: 我不知道它会是什么。
cues.en: I don't know what it will be.

cues.zh: 或者它只是一个恰好能播放媒体的操作系统。
cues.en: Or it'll just be an operating system that happens to be able to play media.

cues.zh: 不。
cues.en: No.

cues.zh: 我们期望看到的是这个：DirectMusic、DirectSound、DirectDraw、Direct3D，对吧？
cues.en: What we expect to see is this, direct music, direct sound, direct draw, direct 3D, right?

cues.zh: 我们预期每样东西都有一个 API，因为我们就是按这种方式组建团队的。
cues.en: We expect to see one API for each of these things, because that is how we structured our teams.

cues.zh: 我们事先就决定要这么做。所以产品也带有这种结构。
cues.en: We decided ahead of time that that's what we were going to do. And so the product has that structure.

cues.zh: 顺便说一句，Windows 当初着手做这件事时，结构也正是这样，对吧？
cues.en: And by the way, this is exactly the structure that Windows had when they sat down to do this, right?

cues.zh: 而且，他们最终还暴露出了组织架构图的其他部分。
cues.en: Now, furthermore, they also ended up with other parts of the org chart exposed.

cues.zh: 我们作为无缘参与设计过程的最终用户，不仅知道这里有个 direct blah，还知道 Direct X 组织，也就是负责那整套东西的整个系统。
cues.en: We not only know as end users who were not privy to the design process, we not only know about the fact that there was this direct blah in here, but the Direct X org, like the whole system that works on that.

cues.zh: 它还给自己立了个品牌，并且有自己发布的那种 SDK，对吧？
cues.en: Also kind of gave itself a brand and has its own like SDK that they ship, right?

cues.zh: 所以整个组织架构图实际上开始暴露出来，我们能在最终产品里看到它。
cues.en: So the the whole org chart actually starts to be exposed, and we can see it in the end product.

cues.zh: 现在这里还有一个额外的变数，我想稍后再讲，所以我就先把它记在这儿，方便回头再说。
cues.en: Now, there's an additional wrinkle here that I want to talk about a little bit later, so I'm just going to, you know, put it in there so that where I can come back to it.

cues.zh: 那就是，如果你看看最终发生的情况，如今这些有点不一样了。
cues.en: And that is, if you look at what ends up happening, nowadays, these are a little bit different.

cues.zh: DirectMusic 已经没了。
cues.en: Direct music went away.

cues.zh: 它现在已经不在了。
cues.en: It's not still there.

cues.zh: 你如果还想用它之类的，仍然可以再分发，但它并没有被积极推广，而且这个组织在 Microsoft 内部已经不存在了。
cues.en: You can still redistribute if you wanted to use it or something, but it's not like actively pushed and the org doesn't exist inside Microsoft anymore.

cues.zh: 它在产品和公司层面都消失了，对吧？
cues.en: It went away in both the product and the company, right?

cues.zh: 现在有了 XAudio，而不是 Direct，呃，而不是 DirectAudio。
cues.en: There's X audio now instead of direct uh instead of direct audio.

cues.zh: 对吧？他们、他们，他们又加了新的。
cues.en: Right? That the they they've added new ones.

cues.zh: 旧的那些还在产品里，但已经没有团队在做 Direct，呃，DirectSound 了，抱歉。
cues.en: The old ones are still in the product, but there isn't like a team working on direct direct sound, sorry.

cues.zh: 呃，我是说 DirectSound。
cues.en: Um, I meant direct sound.

cues.zh: 不是 direct audio，幻灯片上写的就是这个，我说错了。
cues.en: Not direct audio, so it's right in the slide, I said it wrong.

cues.zh: 呃，XAudio、DirectDraw 现在是 Direct2D，但它是完全不同的 API，对吧？
cues.en: Uh, X audio, Direct, uh, Draw is now Direct 2D, but it's a completely different API, right?

cues.zh: 所以 DirectDraw 仍然存在，但 Direct2D 现在作为一种不同的 API 也在。
cues.en: So Direct draw is still in there, but Direct 2D is there now as a different API.

cues.zh: 而 Direct3D 也还在。
cues.en: And Direct 3D is still around.

cues.zh: 那个一直保留至今。
cues.en: That one has has maintained the whole time.

cues.zh: 所以再说一次，现在不用考虑那部分，但我们之后会回来讲。
cues.en: So, again, don't need to think about that part right now, but we're going to come back to it.

cues.zh: 所以请记住，当你在软件中第一次创建这些东西时，这还不是终点。
cues.en: So please remember that, you know, when you first create one of these things in software, that's not the end of the story.

cues.zh: 好。
cues.en: Okay.

cues.zh: 我想在这里传达的是，康威定律告诉我们——如果它最终确实成立的话——组织架构图就是渐近线，对吧？
cues.en: So what I want to try and get across here is that what Conway's law tells us, if it does turn out to be true, is that the org chart is the asymptote, right?

cues.zh: 说到底，你能做到最好的，就是推出一个大致像组织架构图的产品。
cues.en: At the end of the day, the best you can do is put out a product that looks roughly like the org chart.

cues.zh: 现在，它是一条渐近线。
cues.en: Now, it's an asymptote.

cues.zh: 这是你能做到的最好情况。
cues.en: It's the best you can do.

cues.zh: 你能做到最差的情况，其实是更……呃，你知道，更细粒度的那类东西。
cues.en: The worst you can do is actually something much more, uh, you know, granular.

cues.zh: 比如，为了同一个目的，我们有一大堆不同的 API 或东西，因为一个本来没必要这么做的团队没把工作做好。
cues.en: Like something where we have lots of different APIs or things for one purpose because a team that didn't really have to didn't do a very good job.

cues.zh: 于是他们让自己负责的领域变得过于复杂，而且，比方说，在设计上也没做好。
cues.en: So they make too much complexity in their area and don't do a good job on their design, let's say.

cues.zh: 所以它是一条渐近线，是我们能做到的最好情况。
cues.en: So it's an asymptote, it's the best we can do.

cues.zh: 但不一定是我们实际会得到的结果。
cues.en: It's not necessarily what we'll get.

cues.zh: 因为也许这些人不太行，也许这是他们第一次做，或者别的什么，谁知道呢。
cues.en: Because maybe the people weren't very good or maybe it's their first time around or whatever, who knows.

cues.zh: 但这是我们能期望做到的最好情况。
cues.en: But it's the best we can expect to do.

cues.zh: 现在，如果它是一条渐近线，那在我看来，它就很适合放在这里，对吧？
cues.en: Now, if it's an asymptote, to me it fits nicely in here, right?

cues.zh: 我们有过布鲁克斯定律，有过阿姆达尔定律，现在又有了康威定律；它们谈的都是我们在编程中能期望达到的极限。
cues.en: We had Brooks' law, we had Amdal's law, and now we also have Conway's law, and they're all talking about asymptotes in what we can aspire to do in programming.

cues.zh: 布鲁克斯定律告诉我们的是，完成一个项目这件事的极限，对吧？
cues.en: Brooks' law tells us the asymptote for like getting a project done, right?

cues.zh: 它讲的是团队之间的沟通，告诉我们进度安排上能期待什么。
cues.en: It's about the interteam communication. It tells us what we can expect from our schedule.

cues.zh: 阿姆达尔定律告诉我们程序运行时的预期，因为不管计算机变多快，都会有一个天然的渐近极限，它取决于程序里无法并行化的部分，也就是最长的单条依赖链，可以这么说。
cues.en: Amdal's law tells us what we can expect for when the thing runs, because it's just going to tell us no matter how fast computers get, there's going to be this natural asymptote based on what we see in the unparalyzable part of our program, the longest single dependency chain, if you will.

cues.zh: 然后是康威定律，它告诉我们：在极限情况下，如果我们做到最好，产品的软件架构会是什么样？
cues.en: And then we have Conway, which tells us, at the limit, if we do the best we possibly can, what will the software architecture of our product look like?

cues.zh: 答案是，它会呈现出构建它的团队与沟通结构的样子。
cues.en: And the answer is, it will look like the teams and communication structures that built it.

cues.zh: 现在我想强调，康威定律中的“为什么”远比“是什么”重要。
cues.en: Now, I want to emphasize that the why in Conway's law is way more important than the what.

cues.zh: 因为“为什么”可以到处应用，所以只记住“组织架构图会复制自身”这句精辟说法，并不能让你获得完整洞见。
cues.en: Because the why can be applied all over the place, so just remembering the pithy saying of org charts produced copies of themselves doesn't really give you the full insight.

cues.zh: 所以我想做的就是强调一下。
cues.en: And so what I want to do is just emphasize.

cues.zh: 我只是想把它讲得非常清楚。
cues.en: I just like to make it really clear.

cues.zh: 呃，对那些想把它作为一种基础工具记进脑子里的人来说。
cues.en: uh for anyone who, uh, wants to sort of get this into their brain as a fundamental tool.

cues.zh: 我们要说的并不一定是组织架构图在克隆自己。
cues.en: That what we're talking about is not org charts necessarily cloning themselves.

cues.zh: 那是结果。
cues.en: That's the result.

cues.zh: 但必须理解其背后的机制。
cues.en: But the mechanism for that has to be understood.

cues.zh: 机制在于：团队之间的沟通成本高于团队内部；或者推到极限，一个人在敲代码时，和自己沟通基本上是无限快的。
cues.en: The mechanism is that communication between teams is more costly than communication inside teams, or if you want to go to the limit, a single person typing in code communicates with themselves basically infinitely fast.

cues.zh: 我总是知道自己在想什么，对吧？
cues.en: I always know what I am thinking, right?

cues.zh: 所以一个人可以完全自由地按自己的方式把问题想透。
cues.en: So one person has complete latitude to think their way through a problem any way they want to.

cues.zh: 一旦我把这个问题拆成两个人要做的工作，他们之间就必须有某种沟通。
cues.en: As soon as I split that problem into work that two people have to do, there now has to be some communication between them.

cues.zh: 要么他们约定一个接口，要么他们每天、每周或每月沟通，更新彼此的代码如何配合，对吧？
cues.en: Either they agree on an interface or they communicate daily or weekly or monthly to update how their code will work with each other, right?

cues.zh: 或者他们完全不沟通，这意味着他们的代码无法协同演进，也就是说他们之间的边界将始终固定不变。
cues.en: Or they don't communicate at all, which means that their code cannot co-evolve, meaning the boundary between them will remain fixed at all times.

cues.zh: 因为他们甚至都没法彼此交流，呃，你知道，没法以某种方式就下一步做什么达成一致。
cues.en: Because there's no way they can even talk to each other and, uh, you know, have some kind of a way of agreeing on what to do next.

cues.zh: 嗯，再说一次，这里的沟通并不是字面意义上的交谈。它可能意味着我把某些东西提交到源码树里，而你必须把它检出，对吧？
cues.en: Um, and again communication in this case doesn't mean literally talking. It could mean that I check in something to a source tree that you have to check out, right?

cues.zh: 而且这总比自己直接做成本高得多，因为别人不知道我当时在想什么。
cues.en: And that always costs way more than if I were just doing it because you don't know what I was thinking.

cues.zh: 别人不知道我为什么做这些改动。
cues.en: You don't know why I did these changes.

cues.zh: 他们甚至不知道这些改动好不好之类的，对吧？你必须验证这一点，或者达成共识，或者来问我。
cues.en: You don't even know if they're good or whatever, right? You have to validate that or come to an understanding or ask me.

cues.zh: 所以，不管最终怎样，沟通成本越高，那里发生的迭代就越少。
cues.en: So, no matter what ends up happening, the higher the cost of communication, the less iteration will happen there.

cues.zh: 所以你最终看到的是：组织架构图似乎会自我复制，原因并不是“组织架构图会复制自身”这个字面概念。
cues.en: So what you end up with, the reason that org charts seem to replicate themselves is not because of that literal concept that org charts replicate themselves.

cues.zh: 而是因为在任意一个组织架构框内，沟通更快，因此设计迭代也能更快发生。
cues.en: It's because inside any given organizational box, communication is faster, and therefore design iteration can happen more quickly.

cues.zh: 相比之下，如果必须跨框沟通，成本就会上升。
cues.en: than if it has to go across boxes, where the cost is increased.

cues.zh: 所以关键在于创建嵌套的优化域，每往下走一层，设计就能更流畅、更快速地优化。
cues.en: So it's really about creating nested domains of optimization where each level you go down, the design can be optimized more fluidly and more quickly.

cues.zh: 而每往上走一层、每想再往外走一步，比如我需要让这个团队和那边那个团队沟通，如果这两个团队没法直接对接，他们就得一路往上再绕过去，对吧？
cues.en: And each level up you go, each time you try to go further, like for example, if I needed this team here to talk to that team there, they have to go like all the way up and over here, if there isn't a way for those two teams to meet directly, for example, right?

cues.zh: 两件事之间的路径越远，我们就越不能指望它们能探索共同设计。
cues.en: The further the the path is between two things, the less we would expect them to be able to explore shared design.

cues.zh: 而它们问题的解决方案，其实来自一起协作，对吧？
cues.en: where solutions to their problems actually come from doing work together, right?

cues.zh: 所以康威定律不只关乎组织架构图。
cues.en: So Conway's law is not only about org charts.

cues.zh: 它其实讲的是一个基本概念：存在高成本区和低成本区。
cues.en: It's actually just about this fundamental concept that there are high cost and low cost areas.

cues.zh: 如果团队里有优秀的人，低成本的部分最终会被优化；但高成本的部分不行。
cues.en: And the low cost areas will get optimized eventually if you have good people, but the high cost areas cannot be.

cues.zh: 它们就是不行。
cues.en: They just can't be.

cues.zh: 所以最后，我想看看我们今天走到了哪里。
cues.en: So what I'd like to do, finally, is take a look at where we've gotten to now today.

cues.zh: 如果你相信我刚才说的关于康威定律的任何内容，或者我该说，如果你相信康威的论文——我强烈推荐大家都读一读。
cues.en: If you believe anything that I just said about Conway's law, or maybe I should say if you believe Conway's paper, and I highly recommend everyone read it.

cues.zh: 我觉得还不能把它称为定律，因为在软件世界里，我们没有很多证明事情的方法。
cues.en: I don't think we can call it a law yet because we don't have lots of ways of proving things in the software world.

cues.zh: 而且我们其实也不知道如何达成那种共识。
cues.en: And we don't really know how to come to that kind of consensus.

cues.zh: 所以，它被称为康威定律。我有点觉得它可能算是一种定律，但不是像万有引力定律那样的定律。
cues.en: So, it's called Conway's law. I kind of think it probably is sort of a law, but it's not the law like law of gravitation.

cues.zh: 但这是我能想到的唯一一个可能有一天会成为那种定律的。
cues.en: But it's the only one I can think of that might someday be.

cues.zh: 而且我还想说，我已经隐约能看出，它可能还有一种爱因斯坦式的细化，对吧？
cues.en: And furthermore, I would say, I can already sort of see that there's also probably an Einsteinian refinement to it, right?

cues.zh: 如果我们真能确认康威定律是某种真正的基本属性，那很可能也会出现一种……
cues.en: There's probably going to be, if we can really confirm Conway's law is some kind of actual fundamental property.

cues.zh: 到那时我们还会看到，它有一个细化版本，实际上带有额外的细微差别。
cues.en: that we would then also see that there's a refinement to it that actually carries extra nuance.

cues.zh: 所以这就是我现在想讲的。
cues.en: So that's what I want to talk about now.

cues.zh: 我把这一节叫作“Conway's Nightmare”，因为我本来想用这个标题做演讲，但不幸的是，Melvin Conway 并不是人们想到的那个 Conway。
cues.en: I call this section Conway's Nightmare because I wanted to call the talk that, but unfortunately Melvin Conway is not the Conway people think about.

cues.zh: 他们通常想到的是 John Conway，所以我想，如果我把演讲叫作“Conway's Nightmare”，人们会以为要讲 John Conway，其实并不是，我不想误导大家。
cues.en: They usually think about John Conway, so I thought if I called the talk, Conway's Nightmare, people would come thinking there was going to be a lecture on John Conway, which is not, and I didn't want to be misleading.

cues.zh: 所以我觉得，一个神秘的标题总比一个误导性的标题好。
cues.en: So I figured, mysterious title is better than a misleading title.

cues.zh: 于是我选了唯一那个：牢不可破的定律。
cues.en: And I went with the only one, Unbreakable law.

cues.zh: 如果你想在脑子里把它改名为“康威的噩梦”，请随意。
cues.en: If you would like to mentally retitle this, Conway's Nightmare, please do.

cues.zh: 好。
cues.en: Okay.

cues.zh: 并不是说康威不懂软件架构。
cues.en: It's not that Conway didn't know about software architecture.

cues.zh: 他懂。
cues.en: He did.

cues.zh: 所以我不是想说康威当初没考虑过这些问题。
cues.en: So, I'm not trying to say that Conway didn't already think about these things.

cues.zh: 我只是很确定，他没完全预见到事情会怎么发展，因为这篇文章写于1968年，那时的软件和软件开发组织比今天简单得多、也小得多。
cues.en: I'm just pretty sure that he didn't quite foresee where things would go because he was writing this in 1968 when software and software creation organizations were much simpler and smaller than they are today.

cues.zh: 康威绝对懂软件。
cues.en: Conway definitely knew about software.

cues.zh: 他在论文里举了个例子：指派五个人去写一个编译器，结果拿回来一个五遍扫描的编译器，对吧？
cues.en: He gives an example in the paper of, uh, assigning five people to write a compiler and getting back a five pass compiler, right?

cues.zh: 呃，这有点好笑，但你也知道，这正是你会预料到的情况，对吧？
cues.en: Um, which is kind of funny, but, you know, is exactly kind of what you would expect, right?

cues.zh: 他还举了个例子：一个操作系统被拆成的部分，和实际设计它的组织完全对应，对吧？
cues.en: He also gives an example of an operating system being broken down into the same parts as the orgs that actually, uh, designed it, right?

cues.zh: 诸如此类。
cues.en: And things like this.

cues.zh: 所以，他写那篇论文时，肯定在思考计算机和软件。
cues.en: So, he was thinking about computers and software for sure when he wrote the paper.

cues.zh: 但我不认为他当时在想类似这样的情况，对吧？如今，我们每天使用的一些最重要、最基础的软件，比如 Unix 之类的，或者 Windows，呃，你知道，它们的生命周期非常长。
cues.en: But I don't think he was thinking about anything like this, right? Nowadays, some of the most important and foundational software that we use every day, like Unix or something or Windows, uh, you know, their lifespans are massive.

cues.zh: Windows 最初的代码分支是 1985 到 2000 年，对吧？
cues.en: The original code branch of Windows is 1985 to 2000, right?

cues.zh: 后来它和始于 1993 年的 Windows NT 代码分支合并了。
cues.en: That got merged together to produce like with the Windows NT code branch that started in 93.

cues.zh: 这些东西在某种程度上合并到了一起，而且到今天，2022 年，还在运行，对吧？
cues.en: These kind of merged together and are still running today, in 2022, right?

cues.zh: 所以，我们有个东西，至少其中一部分始于 1985 年，一直运行到 2022 年及以后。
cues.en: So, we have something that started at least part of it in 1985 and that's running till 2022 and beyond.

cues.zh: 没有迹象表明明年会有人停止运行 Windows，对吧？
cues.en: There's no sign that anyone's going to stop running Windows next year, right?

cues.zh: 所以这就是一个代码库被使用了四十年。
cues.en: So that's four decades of a code base being in use.

cues.zh: 可能有些想法来自最初版本的 Windows，是那个设计概念空间里的一些小片段。
cues.en: There's some ideas probably from the original version of Windows, some small pieces of that design concept space.

cues.zh: 可能今天仍然存在。
cues.en: are probably still present today.

cues.zh: 当然，Windows 95 时代的所有那些东西今天还在，对吧？
cues.en: Certainly, all the ones from Windows 95 era are there still today, right?

cues.zh: 呃，整个 UI 基础，如果你真去看编程模型，看起来就是那样，对吧？
cues.en: Uh, the entire UI basis, if you actually look at the programming model, looks like that, right?

cues.zh: 它也许这些年在慢慢被替换，但仍然全都在，而且大量东西还在用它，等等等等。
cues.en: It's maybe slowly getting replaced over years, but it's still all there and tons of things use it, etc, etc.

cues.zh: 所以，四十年，40 年的代码库。
cues.en: So, four decades, 40 years, right, of code base.

cues.zh: 所以，我觉得 Conway 没预见到这一点，因为我不知道他怎么可能预见到。
cues.en: And so, what I think Conway didn't foresee, because I don't know how he could have.

cues.zh: 但我觉得 Conway 没预见到的是，他当时想的是，会有一个公司组织架构图来做出一个产品。
cues.en: But what Conway I don't think foresaw is he was thinking that there would be like a company org chart that's going to make a product.

cues.zh: 然后他们做出产品，而产品看起来就像组织架构图，对吧？
cues.en: And they make the product and it looks like the org chart, right?

cues.zh: 所以公司做出产品。
cues.en: So company makes product.

cues.zh: 它们看起来彼此相像。
cues.en: They look like each other.

cues.zh: 然后，如果你把组织架构图改成有些不同的样子，你做了一些调整。
cues.en: And then, if you change the org chart to something somewhat different, you made some changes.

cues.zh: 下次你再做产品时，它就会看起来像那个组织架构图。
cues.en: The next time you make a product, it will then look like that org chart.

cues.zh: 我觉得这就是 Conway 在思考这篇论文时脑子里所想的，对吧？
cues.en: I think that's what Conway had in his head when he was thinking about this paper, right?

cues.zh: 我们改变组织架构图，就改变产品。
cues.en: We change the org chart, we change the product.

cues.zh: 我认为他没预见到的是，这些产品——因为如今软件太容易被留存下来了。
cues.en: What I don't think he foresaw is that these products, because software is so easy to leave around nowadays.

cues.zh: 遗留代码库可不只是常见。
cues.en: Legacy code bases are not just common.

cues.zh: 它们简直就是常态。
cues.en: They're like the rule.

cues.zh: 当你做下一个产品时，更像是上一个产品也被一起延续下来了，对吧？
cues.en: When you do your next product, it's more like the previous product also carries forward, right?

cues.zh: 所以新产品里不仅有老团队和新团队的组织架构，还融合在一起了，对吧？
cues.en: So, new products not only have the org chart from the old team and the new team, like in in them, they merge, right?

cues.zh: 所以你今天做出来的产品，实际上会带上你公司曾经有过的每一个组织架构的影子，都会体现在你当前的设计里。
cues.en: So, a product you produce today will effectively have something in it from like every org chart your company ever had will be in your current design.

cues.zh: 至少在我看来，情况就是这样，对吧？
cues.en: At least that's what it appears to be doing as far as I can see, right?

cues.zh: 唯一能停止这种情况的办法，就是彻底清零。
cues.en: And the only time this stops happening is if you do a clean wipe.

cues.zh: 比如你说，我们要扔掉所有这些代码，从头再来之类的，对吧？
cues.en: If you say we're getting rid of all of this code and we're starting over or something like that, right?

cues.zh: 也就是说，如果你变成了一个新产品或新组织。
cues.en: Says if you became a new product or a new org.

cues.en: Previous teams that existed previously in time were effectively delegated to for parts of the product that still ship today, because it just continues as you ship the same code.

cues.zh: 实际上，真正复制自身的是组织结构图在整个时间维度上的积分。

cues.en: So anytime someone doesn't have enough people to actually solve the whole problem, they just leave all the old stuff in place so that they only have to just solve the new problem, right?

cues.en: This is a class diagram of just the LLVM operator class.

cues.zh: 比如你想把两个数相加，或者左移之类的，明白吧？
cues.en: So like when you want to add two numbers together or shift left or something and see, right?

cues.zh: 这只是 operator 类。
cues.en: It's just the operator class.

cues.zh: 只是 operator 类。
cues.en: Just the operator class.

cues.zh: 我会一直强调这一点，因为这只是 operator 类。
cues.en: I'm going to keep saying that because this is just the operator class.

cues.zh: 这里没有代码。
cues.en: There's no code here.

cues.zh: 这只是一些样板代码，人们得处理、得写下来，基本就是去说明：哦，这个 operator 会指向 conditional operator，有一个左移操作，对吧？
cues.en: This is just boilerplate that people have to deal with and write down to basically specify like, oh, the operator, you know, goes to conditional operator, has a shift left operating right.

cues.zh: 这只是代码内部的代码组织方式。
cues.en: It's just code organization inside the code.

cues.zh: 它并不说明程序如何运行。
cues.en: that does not specify anything about how the program runs.

cues.zh: 它只是程序员额外加进去的东西。
cues.en: It's just there as something that programmers added.

cues.zh: 用来人为约束程序的运作方式。继承层级就是这么回事。
cues.en: to artificially constrain the way the program works. That's what an inheritance hierarchy is.

cues.zh: 它是对程序将来如何运作的人为约束。
cues.en: It's an artificial constraint on how your program is going to work.

cues.zh: 现在如果你把它转过来，对吧？
cues.en: Now if you turn this around, right?

cues.zh: 把它转 90 度，就是一张组织架构图。
cues.en: If you turn it 90 degrees, it's an org chart.

cues.zh: 所以现代编程实践如今实际上已经演变成
cues.en: So modern day programming practices have actually now grown.

cues.zh: 实际上就是组织架构图里套组织架构图。
cues.en: To effectively be org charts inside org charts.

cues.zh: 有一张真实的组织架构图，它会复制到产品上，也就是制造它的人的组织结构。
cues.en: There's an actual org chart, which will replicate itself onto the product, that is the organization of the humans that made it.

cues.zh: 还有一张额外的组织架构图，程序员发明它不为别的，只是因为他们无法把问题的全部复杂性装进脑子里。
cues.en: Then there's an additional org chart that programmers invent for no reason other than they are unable to keep the entire complexity of the problem in their head.

cues.zh: 所以他们人为地把问题拆分开，而这些拆分与设计过程毫无关系。
cues.en: So they invent artificial breakdowns of problems that have nothing to do with the design process.

cues.zh: 因为最优的设计过程会让这一切保持灵活，随着推进找到对产品最好的设计。
cues.en: Because the optimal design process would allow all of this to be fluid to find what design was best for the product as it goes.

cues.zh: 他们人为地把它固定下来。
cues.en: They artificially fix.

cues.zh: 并且给这种变更增加成本。
cues.en: And create increased cost to that change.

cues.zh: 纯粹是为了在头脑中设法应对问题，就造出这样的拆分。
cues.en: By creating one of these for no reason other than mentally trying to grapple with the problem.

cues.zh: 可惜，他们并没有真正意识到自己在这么做，因为他们一直被教导这是好的。
cues.en: Now, unfortunately, they don't really recognize that they're doing this because they've been taught that this is good.

cues.zh: 这样做是好事。
cues.en: This is a good thing to do.

cues.zh: 但实际上，这样做并不好。
cues.en: It's actually not a good thing to do.

cues.zh: 对代码来说，这是坏事。
cues.en: It's a bad thing to do for the code.

cues.zh: 它之所以曾获得“好”的名声，是因为它能把问题拆解，让问题更易管理。
cues.en: The reason that it ever got a reputation for being good is because it is a way of breaking down problems to make them more manageable.

cues.zh: 所以，对于一个个人难以应对的过大问题，这也许是一种必需，对吧？
cues.en: So it may have been a necessity for a problem too large for the person trying to tackle it, right?

cues.zh: 但这恰恰就是现实世界里的组织架构图。
cues.en: But it was exactly what an org chart is in the real world.

cues.zh: 我们做这件事是因为不得不做，而不是因为它真的很好。
cues.en: It's something we do because we had to, not something that's actually good.

cues.zh: 这说明你其实表现不佳，而不是说明你做得很好。
cues.en: This is a sign that you're underachieving, not that you're doing a good job.

cues.zh: 你可能还是得这么做，因为考虑到人脑就是这样，我们想不出更好的办法。
cues.en: You may still have to do it because we can't figure out how to do it any better, given the human brain being what it is.

cues.zh: 但这不该成为值得庆祝的事，对吧？
cues.en: But it shouldn't be cause for celebration, right?

cues.zh: 再说 Conway，因为这篇论文非常了不起，基本上预测了这一切。
cues.en: Now Conway, because this paper is amazing, basically predicted all of this.

cues.zh: 只是更多与管理有关，而不是软件。
cues.en: Just more to do with management than software.

cues.zh: 但他要么当时就在思考软件，要么可能很快就会思考软件，并在他看到面向对象编程等事物出现时，认为软件也具备这些特征。
cues.en: But he either was thinking about software, or would probably soon think about software, as also having these traits as he saw things happen like object oriented programming coming along.

cues.zh: 他说过的一点是，如果设计师面对一个复杂到自己解决不了的问题，通常他们会尝试人为地把它拆成更小的问题，对吧？
cues.en: And so one of the things he says is, if a designer is faced with a problem that is too complex for the designer to solve, what they will generally try to do is artificially break it up into smaller problems, right?

cues.zh: 而且很多时候，他们这么做时，并没有掌握该在哪里拆分所需的必要信息，对吧？
cues.en: And often times they will do this without the necessary information about where those should happen, right?

cues.zh: 因为从定义上说，这个人对问题理解得没那么透彻，所以未必能想清楚：哦，最终设计应该长这样，所以我可以把团队拆成这些部分，分别解决这些问题。
cues.en: Because by definition, the person doesn't understand the problem that well, so they're not necessarily able to figure out, oh, the end design should look something like this, so I can break the teams into these pieces to tackle these problems separately.

cues.zh: 而且我不会产生任何设计成本，因为我已经知道最终设计最优就该是那样，对吧？
cues.en: And I won't incur any design costs because I already know that the end design should be optimially looking like that, right?

cues.zh: 你不是在承担那个风险，你是在让别人承担那个风险。
cues.en: You're not taking that risk, you're letting someone else take that risk.

cues.zh: 你是在让别人承担那个风险，因为那是安全的选择。
cues.en: You're letting someone else take that risk because that's the safe choice.

cues.zh: 所以总而言之，呃，我想用 Melvin Conway 实际写下的那句话来结束。
cues.en: So in conclusion, um, I I would leave you with what with what Melvin Conway actually wrote.

cues.zh: 他的意思基本上是，你看，如果我们想把事情做好，想推进我们的设计能力，那我们需要认识到：我们必须尽可能精简、尽可能灵活。
cues.en: He basically said that look, if we care about doing a good job, and we're trying to push our design ability forward, then what we need to do is understand that we must be as lean and as flexible as possible.

cues.zh: 希望我已经多少向你们表明，如果你研究这类东西，就会意识到，这既适用于组织架构图，也适用于代码库。
cues.en: And as hopefully, I've given you some indication of, if you study this kind of thing, you will realize that that goes for the org chart and the codebase.

cues.zh: 所以，一方面是我们作为人类不得不互相交谈而产生的实际沟通限制；另一方面是我们在代码里做的那些限制其整体优化能力的事情，比如封装，或者使用库——这些通常被认为是好事。
cues.en: So both our actual communication restrictions that we have, because we are humans, to have to talk to each other, and also the things we do in code that restrict its ability to be optimized together, such as encapsulation, or using a library, those sorts of things normally considered good.

cues.zh: 其实它们都是成本；就算我们能神奇地绕过它们，也只会导致更糟的设计。
cues.en: Actually they are all costs that lead to worse designs if we somehow magically could get past them.

cues.zh: 也许我们的大脑做不到，但如果能做到，就会更好。
cues.en: Maybe our brains can't, but if we could, it would be better.

cues.zh: 康威定律告诉了我们这一点，我认为这确实成立。
cues.en: Conway's law tells us so and I think it's really true.

cues.zh: 不幸的是，精简和灵活这两点，几乎和现在大多数人的做法完全相反。
cues.en: And unfortunately, those two things, lean and flexible, are like the opposite of what almost anyone is doing now.

cues.zh: 四万人的组织，使用数十万种不同的组件、库和 Docker 容器，跑在虚拟机里，而虚拟机又运行在 Hypervisor 之上。
cues.en: 40,000 person orgs using hundreds of thousands of different components and libraries and Docker containers inside virtual machines running on top of Hypervisor.

cues.zh: 就像，我们跟精简和灵活完全相反。
cues.en: Like, we're the opposite of lean and flexible.

cues.zh: 我们臃肿、不灵活到了你能想象的极限。
cues.en: We are as fat and unflexible as you could possibly imagine.

cues.zh: 这挺不幸的。
cues.en: And it's kind of unfortunate.

cues.zh: 我觉得康威定律给了我们一个视角，让我们明白为什么不该对此感到高兴。
cues.en: And I think Conway's law kind of gives us a lens to see why we shouldn't be happy about that.

cues.zh: 也许我们正在努力做得更好却做不到，但我们就应该是在努力做得更好却做不到，而不是以为自己做得很好。
cues.en: Maybe we're struggling to do better and can't, but we should be struggling to do better and can't, not thinking that we're doing good.

cues.zh: 因为 Conway 定律多少告诉我们，我们并非如此。
cues.en: Because Conway's law kind of tells us that we aren't.

cues.zh: 最后，我想说，一切都归功于 Melvin Conway 先生，因为他写出了可以说是我读过的最好的软件架构论文；事实上，这似乎对一般意义上的架构都成立，不管是软件还是其他任何东西。
cues.en: And so in closing, I guess I would say, all the thanks go to Mr. Melvin Conway for what is arguably the best software architecture paper I've ever read, and in fact, is just seems to be true about architecture in general, software or anything else.

cues.zh: 我代表今天所有从业者说声抱歉：尽管你警告过我们，并给了我们一个视角去理解自己做错了什么，我们多少还是落入了你设想的噩梦场景——你谈到的所有问题不仅和当初你谈到时一样糟，而且还糟上十倍、百倍、千倍，因为我们真的没做多少努力去尝试克服它们。
cues.en: And I'm I'm sorry on behalf of all of us working today, that even though you warned us and gave us a lens through which to understand what we were doing wrong, we still have sort of ended up in your nightmare scenario, where all of those problems that you talked about are not only as bad as they were when you talked about them, but they are 10 hundreds, thousands of times worse because we're really not doing a lot of work to try and get past them.
